title: 使用 TypeScript 和 Redis 实现滑动窗口限流器
author: SitePoint Team
content:
Rate limiting looks simple until two app instances share one limit and both admit the request that breaks it. This guide builds a distributed sliding-window rate limiter in TypeScript and Redis that stays atomic under concurrency: sorted-set storage, a Lua script for atomic check-and-admit, and dual RPM/TPM quota enforcement with standard rate-limit headers.

How to Build a Distributed Sliding-Window Rate Limiter in TypeScript and Redis

  1. Design a Redis sorted-set key schema encoding cost, timestamp, and a unique suffix per entry to support both RPM and TPM quotas.
  2. Write an atomic Lua script that prunes expired entries, sums remaining costs, conditionally admits the request, and returns remaining capacity and reset time.
  3. Load the Lua script at startup via SCRIPT LOAD and invoke it with EVALSHA, falling back to EVAL on NOSCRIPT errors.
  4. Implement a TypeScript checkLimit method that calls the script once per quota (RPM, then optionally TPM) and merges the results.
  5. Generate IETF-draft-compliant RateLimit-* response headers from the result object.
  6. Wrap the limiter in Express and Hono middleware that extracts client identifiers, sets headers, and returns 429 when denied.
  7. Validate zero over-admission under concurrency by running a k6 burst test with 200 VUs against a 100 RPM limit.
  8. Configure production fail-open/fail-close behavior, Redis Cluster hash tags, and key expiry to match your availability and cost requirements.

Rate limiting in distributed systems is deceptively hard. This article walks through a production-ready distributed sliding-window rate limiter built on Redis sorted sets and an atomic Lua script that eliminates race conditions entirely.

Table of Contents

  • Why Naive Rate Limiting Breaks Under Load
  • Rate-Limiting Algorithms Compared: Why Sliding Window Wins
  • Designing the Lua Script for Atomic Sliding-Window Evaluation
  • Building the TypeScript Wrapper (redis-sliding-limiter)
  • Middleware Integration: Express and Hono
  • Proving Zero Race Conditions: Load Testing with k6
  • Production Considerations and Optimization
  • Next Steps

Why Naive Rate Limiting Breaks Under Load

Rate limiting in distributed systems is deceptively hard. When multiple service instances share state, the most common failure mode is the time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition. A naive implementation reads the current request count from Redis, checks whether the limit has been reached, and then increments the counter in a separate command. Between the read and the write, dozens of concurrent requests can slip through, each independently concluding that capacity remains. Under high concurrency, this pattern routinely over-admits requests -- under high replica counts, over-admission is proportional to the number of concurrent readers between check and write.

This article walks through a production-ready distributed sliding-window rate limiter built on Redis sorted sets and an atomic Lua script that eliminates these race conditions entirely. The implementation supports dual quotas, enforcing both requests-per-minute (RPM) and tokens-per-minute (TPM) simultaneously, and is packaged as a reusable TypeScript library called redis-sliding-limiter. The library exposes framework middleware for both Express and Hono, generates rate-limit response headers following the draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers specification (verify the current draft version at IETF Datatracker before production use), and ships with a k6 load-testing harness that validates zero over-admission under burst conditions.

Under high concurrency, this pattern routinely over-admits requests -- under high replica counts, over-admission is proportional to the number of concurrent readers between check and write.

Prerequisites

  • Redis ≥ 6.2 (required for ZRANGE … WITHSCORES syntax; Redis 7.0+ recommended for improved math.random seeding in Lua scripts)
  • Node.js ≥ 18 (LTS) and TypeScript ≥ 4.7
  • ioredis v5 (v4 has different evalsha argument spreading and script() return types)
  • Express v4 or Hono v3+
  • k6 for load testing
  • CommonJS output ("module": "commonjs" in tsconfig) -- see ESM note in the package structure section

Readers should be comfortable with TypeScript, basic Redis operations, and at least one of Express or Hono.

Rate-Limiting Algorithms Compared: Why Sliding Window Wins

Fixed Window, Leaky Bucket, Token Bucket: Quick Recap

Fixed-window rate limiting divides time into discrete intervals and counts requests per interval. You can implement it quickly, but it suffers from the boundary-burst problem: a client can send the maximum number of requests at the end of one window and the maximum again at the start of the next, effectively doubling throughput across two adjacent seconds.

The leaky bucket algorithm smooths output at a fixed rate, queuing excess requests. This delivers consistent throughput but introduces latency and requires queue management. Token bucket adds flexibility: tokens refill at a steady rate and each request consumes one or more tokens, permitting controlled bursts. However, distributed token bucket implementations must carefully synchronize the token count across replicas, reintroducing the TOCTOU problem.

Sliding Window Log vs. Sliding Window Counter

The sliding-window log approach uses a Redis sorted set to store a timestamped entry for every request. Expired entries outside the current window are pruned on each check, and the remaining cardinality represents the true request count within a continuously sliding time range. This eliminates boundary bursts entirely. The trade-off is memory: each request generates a member in the sorted set. Measuring with MEMORY USAGE on a test key containing 1,000 members and dividing by count yields roughly 100 bytes per entry (including member string, score, and sorted-set overhead); at 10,000 entries that works out to about 1 MB per key. This makes the approach appropriate for API-scale traffic (thousands to tens of thousands of requests per window per key) rather than CDN-scale traffic (millions of requests per second). For most API rate-limiting use cases, the memory overhead is negligible and the correctness guarantees are worth the cost.

The following pseudocode illustrates the sorted-set lifecycle that forms the mental model for the real Lua script:

// Conceptual sliding-window lifecycle using a Redis sorted set
// Each request is stored as a member with its timestamp as the score

// 1. Add the current request's timestamp as the score; encode cost in the member
// ZADD key timestamp "cost:timestamp:randomSuffix"

// 2. Remove all entries outside the sliding window (exclusive lower bound)
// ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key 0 (now - windowMs)   — note the exclusive '(' prefix

// 3. Sum the cost values encoded in each remaining member
//    (For simple RPM counting where cost=1, ZCARD would suffice)

// 4. Compare the sum to the configured limit
// if (sum + cost <= maxAllowed) → ALLOWED, else → DENIED

// 5. Set key expiry to auto-clean after the window elapses
// PEXPIRE key windowMs

Designing the Lua Script for Atomic Sliding-Window Evaluation

Why Lua Scripts Eliminate Race Conditions

Redis executes Lua scripts atomically. Because Redis is single-threaded for command execution (Redis 6.0+ uses I/O threads for network operations, but command processing remains single-threaded), a Lua script runs to completion without any other command interleaving. This means the entire sequence of pruning old entries, counting current entries, conditionally adding a new entry, and setting expiry happens as one indivisible operation. No other client can observe or modify the sorted set between steps.

For performance, Redis caches compiled Lua scripts by their SHA1 hash. The EVALSHA command executes a previously loaded script by hash, avoiding the overhead of transmitting the full script text on every invocation. The TypeScript wrapper loads the script once at startup and uses EVALSHA for all subsequent calls. If Redis restarts (flushing the script cache), the wrapper catches the resulting NOSCRIPT error and falls back to EVAL, re-caching the SHA automatically.

A common misconception is that MULTI/EXEC transactions provide equivalent atomicity. They do not. MULTI/EXEC queues commands and executes them sequentially, but the results of earlier commands in the transaction are not available to later commands within the same transaction. Read-then-write logic, which is exactly what rate limiting requires, cannot be expressed in a MULTI/EXEC block without WATCH, and WATCH-based optimistic locking retries under contention, degrading performance at precisely the moment it matters most.

The sliding_window.lua Script, Line by Line

The script accepts one key (the sorted-set key for a given consumer and quota type) and four arguments: the current timestamp in milliseconds, the window duration in milliseconds, the maximum allowed count, and the cost of the current request (1 for RPM counting, or a token weight for TPM counting).

The score of each sorted-set member is the request's timestamp in milliseconds, which enables temporal pruning via ZREMRANGEBYSCORE. The cost value (1 for RPM, N for TPM) is encoded in the member string and parsed during the summation loop.

-- scripts/sliding_window.lua
-- Atomic sliding-window rate limiter using a sorted set
-- KEYS[1]: the rate-limit key, e.g. "rl:{userId}:rpm"
-- ARGV[1]: now_ms      — current time in milliseconds
-- ARGV[2]: window_ms   — sliding window duration in milliseconds
-- ARGV[3]: max_count   — maximum allowed sum within the window
-- ARGV[4]: cost        — weight of this request (1 for RPM, N for TPM)

local key        = KEYS[1]
local now_ms     = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window_ms  = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local max_count  = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost       = tonumber(ARGV[4])

-- Remove all entries that have fallen outside the sliding window.
-- Use exclusive lower boundary '(' so entries exactly at window_start are retained.
local window_start = now_ms - window_ms
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, '(' .. window_start)

-- Sum the cost encoded in each remaining member's string
-- Member format: "cost:timestamp:seq"
local members = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', key, '-inf', '+inf')
local current_sum = 0
for i = 1, #members do
  local entry_cost = tonumber(string.match(members[i], '^(%d+):'))
  if entry_cost then
    current_sum = current_sum + entry_cost
  end
end

-- Check whether adding this request would exceed the limit
if current_sum + cost > max_count then
  -- Denied: compute reset time from the oldest entry still in the window.
  -- ZRANGEBYSCORE with WITHSCORES returns a flat array: {member, score, ...}
  -- With LIMIT 0 1 the result is {member, score}.
  local oldest = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', key, '-inf', '+inf', 'WITHSCORES', 'LIMIT', 0, 1)
  -- oldest[1] = member string, oldest[2] = score string
  local oldest_score = oldest[2] and tonumber(oldest[2])
  local reset_ms = oldest_score
    and (oldest_score + window_ms)
    or  (now_ms + window_ms)
  -- Set expiry on denied path to ensure cleanup even if no further requests arrive
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window_ms)
  return {0, max_count - current_sum, math.floor(reset_ms)}
end

-- Allowed: add the new entry with score = timestamp, cost encoded in member.
-- Use a Redis-side per-key sequence counter as the unique suffix to avoid
-- member collisions on Redis <7.0 (where the Lua random seed is fixed).
local seq = redis.call('INCR', key .. ':seq')
redis.call('PEXPIRE', key .. ':seq', window_ms)
local member = tostring(cost) .. ':' .. now_ms .. ':' .. seq
redis.call('ZADD', key, now_ms, member)

-- Set key expiry so it auto-cleans after the window passes
redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window_ms)

local remaining = max_count - (current_sum + cost)
local reset_ms  = now_ms + window_ms

return {1, remaining, math.floor(reset_ms)}

The script returns a three-element array: [allowed (0|1), remaining capacity, reset timestamp in ms]. Using the member string to encode cost while keeping the score as a timestamp allows the same script to handle both RPM (cost = 1 per request) and TPM (cost = number of tokens consumed) quotas, while ensuring that temporal pruning via ZREMRANGEBYSCORE works correctly. The math.floor call on reset_ms ensures the return value is always a Redis integer, preventing ioredis from returning it as a bulk string.

Note on member uniqueness: The script uses a Redis-side per-key sequence counter (INCR key:seq) as the unique suffix for member strings. This eliminates the collision risk present in Redis < 7.0, where math.random uses a fixed seed per process and concurrent requests at the same millisecond can produce identical member strings, causing one ZADD to silently overwrite the other.

Handling Dual RPM/TPM Quotas

Enforcing both RPM and TPM requires two sorted-set keys per consumer, for example rl:{userId}:rpm and rl:{userId}:tpm. The TypeScript wrapper invokes the Lua script twice in sequence, once for each quota. If either check fails, the request is denied.

Important: The two-call approach is not fully atomic across both quotas. Each individual invocation is atomic, but if the RPM check passes and writes its entry and the TPM check subsequently denies the request, the RPM counter permanently increments for a request that the TPM check ultimately rejects. Over time, this causes the RPM quota to drift below its true value. For strict accuracy, combine both checks into a single Lua script accepting two key/limit pairs. The two-call approach shown here is simpler and acceptable when minor RPM drift is tolerable, but operators should be aware of this trade-off.

Building the TypeScript Wrapper (redis-sliding-limiter)

Package Structure and Configuration Interface

The library follows a standard layout: packages/redis-sliding-limiter/src/ contains the TypeScript source, scripts/ holds the Lua file, and tests/ contains both unit and load tests.

Build configuration requirement: The tsconfig must use "outDir": "dist" and "rootDir": "src" so that the compiled JavaScript in dist/ can resolve ../scripts/sliding_window.lua relative to the package root. For ESM projects ("type": "module" in package.json), __dirname is not available -- use the following shim before the readFileSync call:

import { fileURLToPath } from 'url';
import { dirname } from 'path';

const __dirname = dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));

The configuration interface and class constructor handle ioredis connection management and Lua script loading:

// src/types.ts
import type Redis from 'ioredis';

export interface LimiterConfig {
  /** Sliding window duration in milliseconds */
  windowMs: number;
  /** Maximum requests allowed per window (RPM quota) */
  maxRequests: number;
  /** Maximum token weight allowed per window (TPM quota, optional) */
  maxTokens?: number;
  /** Key prefix for Redis keys */
  keyPrefix: string;
  /** ioredis client instance */
  redis: Redis;
  /** Behavior on Redis errors: 'allow' passes the request, 'deny' blocks it.
   *  Must be explicitly set. If omitted and Redis fails, checkLimit will throw. */
  onError: 'allow' | 'deny';
}

export interface RateLimitResult {
  allowed: boolean;
  remaining: number;
  resetAt: Date;
  retryAfterMs: number;
}

// src/limiter.ts
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { resolve, dirname } from 'path';
import type Redis from 'ioredis';
import type { LimiterConfig, RateLimitResult } from './types';

export class SlidingWindowLimiter {
  private readonly config: LimiterConfig;
  private readonly redis: Redis;
  private scriptSha: string | null = null;
  private loadPromise: Promise<void> | null = null;
  private scriptSource: string | null = null;

  constructor(config: LimiterConfig) {
    this.config = config;
    this.redis = config.redis;
  }

  async loadScript(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.loadPromise) return this.loadPromise;
    this.loadPromise = (async () => {
      // ESM-safe: resolve path inside async context where shim can be applied
      const scriptDir = typeof __dirname !== 'undefined'
        ? __dirname
        : dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
      const src = readFileSync(
        resolve(scriptDir, '../scripts/sliding_window.lua'),
        'utf-8'
      );
      this.scriptSource = src;
      this.scriptSha = await this.redis.script('LOAD', src) as string;
    })().catch((err) => { this.loadPromise = null; throw err; });
    return this.loadPromise;
  }
}

You MUST call await limiter.loadScript() before any checkLimit() call. Failure to do so will cause checkLimit to throw, as scriptSource will be null.

The checkLimit Method

The core method accepts an identifier string (user ID, API key, or IP address) and an optional token cost. It constructs the Redis key, calls the Lua script via EVALSHA, and maps the raw response into a typed RateLimitResult. If EVALSHA fails with a NOSCRIPT error (e.g., after a Redis restart), the method transparently falls back to EVAL and re-caches the script SHA.

The identifier is sanitized to remove { and } characters, which would interfere with Redis Cluster hash-tag extraction and could cause RPM and TPM keys for the same user to land on different shards:

// src/limiter.ts — checkLimit method on SlidingWindowLimiter

async checkLimit(
  identifier: string,
  tokenCost: number = 1
): Promise<RateLimitResult> {
  if (!this.scriptSource) {
    throw new Error('loadScript() must be called before checkLimit()');
  }

  // Sanitize identifier to prevent Redis Cluster hash-tag corruption
  const safeIdentifier = identifier.replace(/[{}]/g, '_');
  const rpmKey = `${this.config.keyPrefix}:{${safeIdentifier}}:rpm`;
  const nowMs = Date.now();
  const rpmArgs = [
    nowMs.toString(),
    this.config.windowMs.toString(),
    this.config.maxRequests.toString(),
    '1',  // RPM always counts requests, not token weight
  ];

  let rpmResult: [number, number, number];
  try {
    rpmResult = await this.execScript(rpmKey, rpmArgs);
  } catch (err) {
    return this.handleError(err, nowMs);
  }

  const [rpmAllowed, rpmRemaining, rpmResetMs] = rpmResult;

  if (rpmAllowed !== 1) {
    return {
      allowed: false,
      remaining: Math.max(0, rpmRemaining),
      resetAt: new Date(rpmResetMs),
      retryAfterMs: Math.max(0, rpmResetMs - nowMs),
    };
  }

  // If maxTokens is configured, run a second check against the TPM key.
  // Note: RPM entry has already been written at this point. If TPM denies,
  // the RPM count is permanently incremented for this denied request.
  if (this.config.maxTokens !== undefined) {
    const tpmKey = `${this.config.keyPrefix}:{${safeIdentifier}}:tpm`;
    const tpmArgs = [
      nowMs.toString(),
      this.config.windowMs.toString(),
      this.config.maxTokens.toString(),
      tokenCost.toString(),
    ];

    let tpmResult: [number, number, number];
    try {
      tpmResult = await this.execScript(tpmKey, tpmArgs);
    } catch (err) {
      return this.handleError(err, nowMs);
    }

    const [tpmAllowed, tpmRemaining, tpmResetMs] = tpmResult;
    if (tpmAllowed !== 1) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        remaining: Math.max(0, tpmRemaining),
        resetAt: new Date(tpmResetMs),
        retryAfterMs: Math.max(0, tpmResetMs - nowMs),
      };
    }

    // Surface the tighter of the two remaining quotas
    return {
      allowed: true,
      remaining: Math.max(0, Math.min(rpmRemaining, tpmRemaining)),
      resetAt: new Date(rpmResetMs),
      retryAfterMs: 0,
    };
  }

  return {
    allowed: true,
    remaining: Math.max(0, rpmRemaining),
    resetAt: new Date(rpmResetMs),
    retryAfterMs: 0,
  };
}

private parseScriptResult(raw: unknown): [number, number, number] {
  if (!Array.isArray(raw) || raw.length < 3) {
    throw new Error(`Unexpected Lua response: ${JSON.stringify(raw)}`);
  }
  const [allowed, remaining, resetMs] = raw.map(Number);
  if (isNaN(allowed) || isNaN(remaining) || isNaN(resetMs)) {
    throw new Error(`Non-numeric Lua response: ${JSON.stringify(raw)}`);
  }
  return [allowed, remaining, resetMs];
}

private async execScript(
  key: string,
  args: string[]
): Promise<[number, number, number]> {
  try {
    const raw = this.scriptSha
      ? await this.redis.evalsha(this.scriptSha, 1, key, ...args)
      : await this.redis.eval(this.scriptSource!, 1, key, ...args);
    return this.parseScriptResult(raw);
  } catch (err: any) {
    if (err?.message?.includes('NOSCRIPT')) {
      const raw = await this.redis.eval(this.scriptSource!, 1, key, ...args);
      this.scriptSha = await this.redis.script('LOAD', this.scriptSource!) as string;
      return this.parseScriptResult(raw);
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

private handleError(err: unknown, nowMs: number): RateLimitResult {
  if (this.config.onError === 'allow') {
    return {
      allowed: true,
      remaining: 0,
      resetAt: new Date(nowMs + this.config.windowMs),
      retryAfterMs: 0,
    };
  }
  // onError === 'deny'
  return {
    allowed: false,
    remaining: 0,
    resetAt: new Date(nowMs + this.config.windowMs),
    retryAfterMs: this.config.windowMs,
  };
}

Generating IETF RateLimit Response Headers

Following the draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers specification, the library provides a utility that converts a RateLimitResult into HTTP headers suitable for inclusion in any response. Header names follow the RateLimit-Limit / RateLimit-Remaining / RateLimit-Reset convention from earlier drafts; verify field names against the current draft version at IETF Datatracker before production deployment, as later revisions restructure these into a single RateLimit structured-field header.

// src/headers.ts
import type { RateLimitResult } from './types';

export function toRateLimitHeaders(
  result: RateLimitResult,
  limit: number
): Record<string, string> {
  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    'RateLimit-Limit': limit.toString(),
    'RateLimit-Remaining': Math.max(0, result.remaining).toString(),
    'RateLimit-Reset': Math.ceil(result.resetAt.getTime() / 1000).toString(),
  };
  if (!result.allowed) {
    headers['Retry-After'] = Math.ceil(result.retryAfterMs / 1000).toString();
  }
  return headers;
}

Middleware Integration: Express and Hono

Express Middleware Wrapper

The factory function wraps the limiter in standard Express middleware, extracting the client identifier via a caller-supplied function and returning 429 Too Many Requests when the limit is exceeded:

// src/middleware/express.ts
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import type { SlidingWindowLimiter } from '../limiter';
import { toRateLimitHeaders } from '../headers';

export function createRateLimitMiddleware(
  limiter: SlidingWindowLimiter,
  identifierFn: (req: Request) => string,
  limit: number
) {
  return async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
    const identifier = identifierFn(req);

    let result;
    try {
      result = await limiter.checkLimit(identifier);
    } catch (err) {
      // checkLimit handles onError internally; this catch guards
      // against unexpected errors not covered by onError logic
      next(err);
      return;
    }

    const headers = toRateLimitHeaders(result, limit);
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(headers)) {
      res.setHeader(key, value);
    }

    if (!result.allowed) {
      res.status(429).json({
        error: 'Too Many Requests',
        retryAfterMs: result.retryAfterMs,
      });
      return;
    }

    next();
  };
}

Hono Middleware Wrapper

The equivalent middleware for Hono uses its Context API. Hono runs on Bun, Deno, and Node.js. As of June 2024, ioredis compatibility with Bun's Node.js compatibility layer is unverified; test against your specific Bun version before production use, or use the redis npm package as an alternative with broader runtime compatibility.

// src/middleware/hono.ts
import type { Context, Next } from 'hono';
import type { SlidingWindowLimiter } from '../limiter';
import { toRateLimitHeaders } from '../headers';

export function honoRateLimitMiddleware(
  limiter: SlidingWindowLimiter,
  identifierFn: (c: Context) => string,
  limit: number
) {
  return async (c: Context, next: Next) => {
    const identifier = identifierFn(c);

    let result;
    try {
      result = await limiter.checkLimit(identifier);
    } catch (err) {
      // Fallback for unexpected errors beyond onError handling
      return c.json({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }, 500);
    }

    const headers = toRateLimitHeaders(result, limit);
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(headers)) {
      c.header(key, value);
    }

    if (!result.allowed) {
      return c.json(
        { error: 'Too Many Requests', retryAfterMs: result.retryAfterMs },
        429
      );
    }

    await next();
  };
}

Proving Zero Race Conditions: Load Testing with k6

Test Scenario Design

The critical claim of this library is that it never over-admits requests, regardless of concurrency. To test this, the scenario uses 200 virtual users, each sending 10 requests in a 1-second burst against an endpoint rate-limited to 100 RPM. That produces 2,000 total requests. If the limiter is correct, exactly 100 should receive HTTP 200, and the remaining 1,900 should receive HTTP 429. Any result where more than 100 requests succeed indicates a race condition.

The critical claim of this library is that it never over-admits requests, regardless of concurrency.

k6 Script and Results Analysis

The k6 test requires a running API server on localhost:3000 with the rate-limiting middleware configured for 100 RPM using a shared identifier (e.g., a fixed X-API-Key header value). Start your server before running the test. Important: Flush the test key from Redis before each run to ensure deterministic results (e.g., redis-cli DEL "rl:{shared-test-key}:rpm"), or use a unique key per test run via a timestamp suffix.

// tests/burst_test.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Counter } from 'k6/metrics';

const allowed = new Counter('allowed_requests');
const denied  = new Counter('denied_requests');

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:3000';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    burst: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 200,
      iterations: 10,
      maxDuration: '10s',
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/api/test`, {
    headers: { 'X-API-Key': 'shared-test-key' },
  });

  if (res.status === 200) {
    allowed.add(1);
  } else if (res.status === 429) {
    denied.add(1);
  }
}

Running this test against a correctly configured server should produce the following results:

A zero over-admission count confirms that the Lua script's atomic execution prevents any TOCTOU race, even under extreme concurrency.

Edge Cases Verified

Window rollover mid-burst is handled naturally by the sorted-set pruning logic: entries that fall outside the window boundary are removed before counting, so a burst that spans two windows never double-counts. Redis connection failure behavior depends on the onError configuration. With onError: 'allow', the middleware passes the request through when Redis is unreachable, implementing fail-open semantics suitable for systems where availability takes priority over strict rate enforcement. With onError: 'deny', requests are blocked when Redis is unavailable -- appropriate for systems where over-admission is more dangerous than brief downtime. You must explicitly configure onError: 'deny' in LimiterConfig; see the type definition above.

Production Considerations and Optimization

Memory Management and Key Expiry

Every invocation of the Lua script calls PEXPIRE on the sorted-set key (on both the allowed and denied paths), ensuring that keys are automatically cleaned up after the window elapses even if no further requests arrive for that consumer. Keep sorted-set member values compact: the cost:timestamp:seq format (e.g., 1:1718900000000:42) produces members around 22 bytes long, compared to 36 bytes for a UUID -- a meaningful saving when multiplied across thousands of entries per key.

If a key grows beyond roughly 10,000 entries, profile the Lua script's O(N) member iteration on your hardware; the iteration cost rises linearly, and at high member counts it can add noticeable latency per call. For windows that large, consider a separate hash-field structure to track cumulative cost. Operators can monitor per-key overhead at any time with MEMORY USAGE rl:{userId}:rpm.

Redis Cluster and Multi-Node Deployments

When running Redis in cluster mode, all keys accessed within a single Lua script invocation must reside on the same shard. The hash-tag syntax {userId} in the key pattern rl:{userId}:rpm ensures that Redis hashes only the content inside the braces, co-locating both the RPM and TPM keys for a given user on the same shard. The library sanitizes identifier values to remove { and } characters, preventing user-supplied input from interfering with Redis's hash-tag extraction. Cross-region Redis deployments introduce latency that directly adds to every rate-limited request's response time. For latency-sensitive applications, the Redis instance should be co-located in the same region as the API servers, accepting that rate limits are enforced per-region rather than globally.

Fail-Open vs. Fail-Close Strategies

The onError configuration option in LimiterConfig governs behavior during Redis outages. Neither strategy is universally correct. Fail-open preserves availability at the risk of allowing traffic spikes to reach downstream services unthrottled. Fail-close preserves protection at the cost of rejecting legitimate traffic during infrastructure issues. For mission-critical APIs with expensive downstream resources (such as LLM inference endpoints billed per token), fail-close is the safer default unless your SLA penalizes downtime more than over-admission. Wrapping the Redis connection in a circuit-breaker pattern, opening the circuit after a configurable number of consecutive failures and periodically probing for recovery, prevents cascading latency when Redis is slow rather than fully down.

For mission-critical APIs with expensive downstream resources (such as LLM inference endpoints billed per token), fail-close is the safer default unless your SLA penalizes downtime more than over-admission.

Next Steps

Redis sorted sets combined with atomic Lua execution give you a distributed sliding-window rate limiter with strong correctness guarantees under concurrency. The redis-sliding-limiter package encapsulates this pattern in a reusable TypeScript library with framework middleware, rate-limit response headers, and a load-testing harness that validates zero over-admission.

Natural extensions include per-endpoint limit configuration (using route patterns in the Redis key), dynamic quota tiers loaded from a database at request time, and Prometheus metrics exporting for rate-limit hit rates and remaining capacity. The k6 test suite works as both a correctness validation and a regression safety net as the limiter evolves. To see these guarantees hold under real load, point the burst test at a local Redis instance and wire the middleware into an existing API.

summary: 本技术指南详细介绍了生产级分布式限流器的实现，旨在解决分布式系统中常见的 TOCTOU（检查时间到使用时间）竞态条件。通过利用 Redis 有序集合（Sorted Sets）和原子化 Lua 脚本，作者实现了一种滑动窗口算法，消除了固定窗口方法中常见的边界突发流量问题。该方案支持双重配额强制执行（每分钟请求数 RPM 和每分钟 Token 数 TPM），提供符合 IETF 标准的限流响应头，并包含针对 Express 和 Hono 的中间件集成。文章还通过 k6 负载测试验证了实现的正确性，证明在高并发环境下实现了零超额准入。

mainPoints.point: 通过 Lua 脚本的原子执行消除分布式竞态条件
mainPoints.explanation: 分布式系统中简单的「先读后写」模式会导致超额准入。由于 Redis 原子化地执行 Lua 脚本，因此清理过期条目、计算当前成本和准入请求的整个过程作为一个不可分割的操作完成。

mainPoints.point: 滑动窗口日志通过消除边界突发流量优于固定窗口计数器
mainPoints.explanation: 固定窗口在时间间隔边界可能会允许双倍的吞吐量，而滑动窗口日志使用有序集合跟踪时间戳，确保在连续移动的时间范围内进行精确计数。

mainPoints.point: 支持 RPM 和 TPM 双重配额可实现灵活的 API 使用限制
mainPoints.explanation: 该实现为请求计数（RPM）和 Token 权重（TPM）使用了独立的有序集合键，使系统能够同时限制调用频率和消耗的数据/Token 数量。

mainPoints.point: 生产级集成需要谨慎处理 Redis Cluster 和脚本缓存
mainPoints.explanation: 指南强调使用 EVALSHA 以提升性能，为 NOSCRIPT 错误实现回退逻辑，并对标识符进行清洗，以确保 Redis Cluster 分片之间哈希标签的一致性。
